hypothesis: The best config is already at 3 calls (inspect, one big write+build+smoke, summary). The remaining cost is about 8.9k tokens of fixed built-in system prompt and tool schemas, re-read on each of 3 calls, plus 6.3k of task prompt. Replacing the built-in Claude Code system prompt (systemPromptMode "replace") with a ~500-token prompt that keeps the 3-call workflow should cut roughly 4-6k tokens per call without changing behaviour.
changeSummary: Set claudeCode.systemPromptMode to "replace" (keeping tools [Bash, Read, Edit, Write]) and rewrite system-prompt.md as a compact standalone prompt. The prompt describes the autonomous setting, the tools, and the low-call workflow: one safe exploration call plus a design image Read, then write all files in one call, with build and API smoke test in that same call. It also says to avoid failing globs and give a short summary.

+Task context:
+- The specification (requirements, API contract, design tokens) is already included in the task prompt, and the reference design images are /spec/design.png and /spec/design-mobile.png. Do not re-read spec files that are already inline.
+- There is no network access and no curl. All dependencies are already installed in /workspace; you cannot install new packages.
+
+How to work (every model call re-sends the whole conversation, so fewer calls means lower cost):
+- Start with ONE exploratory Bash call that lists the starter files and prints the small config files you need (package.json, the existing backend entry, the vite config, index.html, main entry). Join commands with `;` and avoid globs that may match nothing, so the call cannot fail on a missing path. In the same turn, view the desktop design image with Read.
+- Then write each source file completely in a single call, using Bash heredocs for several files at once (or Write). Plan the whole app first, then emit it once; do not iterate file by file, and avoid Edit unless fixing a small bug.
+- In that same Bash call, after writing the files, run `npm run build`, start the server in the background on a spare port with a temporary DATABASE_PATH, exercise the API with a small Node script using fetch (including error cases and the `/` frontend route), print only failures or short summaries, then stop the server. Pipe noisy output through `tail`.
+- Only fix and re-run if something actually failed. Do not re-read files you just wrote.
+- Follow the spec's exact accessible names, roles, texts, status codes, error envelope and ordering rules.
+- When everything builds and works, stop and reply with a very short summary (two or three sentences).
evidence: Profile for run-20261115-121604-fcbbc8 (best config, 64.7k, 3 calls): the first-call context is 15.2k, of which the task prompt is about 6.29k, so fixed system+tools is about 8.88k per call. Fixed overhead is about 41% of total, and cache reads are 50.5k (78%). The timeline is #1 Bash inspect + Read design.png, #2 a single Bash heredoc of 14.3k chars that wrote the app, and #3 the summary. The 4-call outlier run-20261115-121250-ddbd47 (82.9k) lost one whole call (17.3k) to a failed first Bash (`cat vite.co...` on a missing path), a 'error-retry' waste signal. So the prompt also advises exploration commands that cannot fail. The Skill tool is already gone since exp-0007, so the only remaining fixed block is the built-in prompt, which "replace" mode swaps for about 2KB of text. No past experiment tried replace mode (exp-0001 to exp-0007 were baseline, tools whitelist, or hook runs).
expectedSavings: The built-in prompt is probably about 4-6k tokens of the 8.9k fixed prefix, and the new prompt is about 0.5k. That saves about 4-5k per call across 3 calls, roughly 12-15k from 64.7k (about 20%). It also helps in the occasional 4th call, which would save about 5k more, and the failed-first-call advice reduces variance. Main risks: (1) without the built-in guidance the model might do more exploration or verification turns, and each extra turn costs at least 25k; (2) the built-in prompt may carry tool-use conventions, such as the heredoc-in-Bash habit, that the model now has to infer. The prompt states the workflow explicitly to mitigate both. Visual and API checks come from the model's one-shot app, which should be unchanged since the spec is in the task prompt.
